gloss: eye; sight, regard, judgment; spring of water
summary: עַיִן is the eye, and so whatever the eye does or shows: sight, eyes lifted up or opened to see, the desire that goes after what it sees, and the judgment of the one who looks, so that a thing is right or evil “in the eyes of” a man or of Yahweh (Gen 6:8; Jdg 17:6; Num 15:39). The same word is a spring of water, the eye of the ground at which water is drawn (Gen 16:7; 24:13), and מַעְיָן is the spring or fountain, from the fountains of the great deep broken open at the flood to the wells of salvation (Gen 7:11; Isa 12:3). Its one verb is Saul eyeing David with jealous suspicion (1Sa 18:9). Arabic ʿayn, Akkadian īnu, Ugaritic ʿn, Sabaic ʿyn and Syriac ʿaynā are all both eye and spring.

words.gloss: eye; sight; regard, judgment; look, appearance; spring
words.summary: One of the commonest nouns of scripture, usually dual עֵינַיִם. Over a third of its uses are the phrases בְּעֵינֵי “in the eyes of” and לְעֵינֵי “before the eyes of”, where the eye stands for a person's judgment or presence. As “spring” it has the plural עֲיָנוֹת.

senses.definition: The eye of a man or beast: it can be struck and destroyed, bored out, dimmed by age, or have a defect in it; Yahweh formed it.

evidence.note: A man who strikes the עֵין of his servant and destroys it must let him go free “for his eye”.
Moses at a hundred and twenty: “his eye was not dim”.
“He who formed the עַיִן, shall he not see?” beside the ear.
A defect in his eye bars a son of Aaron from offering.
Isaac's eyes were too dim to see.
Nahash's terms: to bore out every right eye.
The Philistines bored out Samson's eyes.
Zedekiah's eyes put out.
“The hearing ear and the seeing eye, Yahweh has made both of them.”

senses.definition: The eye as what weeps and runs with tears in grief.

evidence.note: “Oh that my head were waters and my eye a fountain (מְקוֹר) of tears!”: the eye likened to a spring.
“My eye, my eye runs down with water.”
Streams of water run down my eyes because they do not keep your law.
“My eye wastes away from affliction.”

senses.gloss: sight; eyes lifted up or opened to see
senses.definition: The eye as seeing: to lift up the eyes is to look, and to have the eyes opened or uncovered is to see what was there but not seen.

evidence.note: Abraham “lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, a ram”.
Yahweh uncovered Balaam's eyes, and he saw the angel standing in the way.
“Yahweh, open his eyes that he may see”: the young man sees the horses and chariots of fire.
Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the plain of the Jordan.
“Your eyes will be opened”; and in 3:7 they were, and they knew they were naked.
“By the hearing of the ear I had heard of you, but now my eye sees you”: seeing set against hearsay.
“You, Yahweh, are seen eye to eye.”
As the eyes of servants to the hand of their masters, so our eyes to Yahweh.
Jesus lifted up his eyes and spoke to the Father: the same gesture in the New Testament.

senses.definition: Eyes that truly see are understanding, given or withheld by God; a people that will not turn has eyes and does not see.

evidence.note: “Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day”; quoted in Rom 11:8.
“Shut his eyes, lest he see with his eyes … and understand with his heart, and turn”; quoted in Mat 13:15, Jhn 12:40, Act 28:27.
“Who have eyes and do not see”; echoed in Mrk 8:18.
“Uncover my eyes, that I may behold wonderful things out of your law.”
The eyes of the blind opened when Yahweh comes.
“Blessed are your eyes, for they see.”

senses.gloss: in the eyes of: in one's judgment, regard
senses.definition: בְּעֵינֵי, “in the eyes of”: how a thing looks to someone, so their judgment of it and their regard for a person. Favour is found in someone's eyes; a man does what is right in his own eyes; Israel did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh.

evidence.note: “Noah found favour (חֵן) in the eyes of Yahweh.”
No king in Israel: “each man did what was right in his own eyes.”
“The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but he who listens to counsel is wise.”
“We were in our own eyes as grasshoppers, and so we were in their eyes.”
The generation “that did evil in the eyes of Yahweh”.
“Do what is right and good in the eyes of Yahweh.”
Her mistress was made light in Hagar's eyes.
“Why have I not found favour in your eyes?”
“A thousand years in your eyes are as yesterday.”
“Do not be wise in your own eyes.”
“Favour and good understanding in the eyes of God and man”; echoed in Rom 12:17 and 2Co 8:21.
“It is marvellous in our eyes”; quoted in Mat 21:42 and Mrk 12:11.

senses.gloss: before the eyes of: in the sight of, publicly
senses.definition: לְעֵינֵי, “to the eyes of”: done where someone sees it, in their presence, so that they are witnesses.

evidence.note: Moses and Aaron did not believe Yahweh, “to sanctify me in the eyes of the sons of Israel”.
Joseph took Simeon and bound him before their eyes.
“Speak to the rock before their eyes.”
All that Yahweh did in Egypt before your eyes.
The red heifer burned before the priest's eyes.
Israel went out of Egypt with a high hand before the eyes of all the Egyptians.
“I will be sanctified in you before the eyes of the nations.”

senses.definition: To be eyes to others is to see for them: Hobab, who knew the wilderness and where Israel should camp, was asked to be their eyes; Job was eyes to the blind.

evidence.note: “You know our camping in the wilderness, and you shall be to us for eyes (לְעֵינָיִם).”
“I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame.”

senses.gloss: the eye as desire and disposition; good eye, evil eye
senses.definition: The eye goes after what it covets and is never satisfied; and it shows the heart's disposition toward others: a good eye is generous, an evil eye grudging, and an eye that will not pity shows no mercy.

evidence.note: The fringes, “that you go not about after your own heart and your own eyes, after which you go astray”.
“He who is good of eye shall be blessed, for he gives of his bread to the poor.”
Lest “your eye be evil against your poor brother, and you give him nothing”.
“Do not eat the bread of one evil of eye.”
The grave and destruction are never satisfied, “and the eyes of man are never satisfied”.
“I made a covenant with my eyes; how then should I look upon a virgin?”
“Your eye shall not pity him.”
“Is your eye evil because I am good?”: the same idiom for grudging.
“The lust of the eyes.”

senses.gloss: the eyes of Yahweh: his sight, watch and care
senses.definition: Yahweh's eyes see in every place: they test men, watch the evil and the good, rest on the land and on those who fear him, and keep his people as the pupil of the eye.

evidence.note: “The eyes of Yahweh are in every place, watching the evil and the good.”
A land Yahweh cares for: “the eyes of Yahweh your God are always on it, from the beginning of the year to its end”.
“Yahweh's throne is in heaven; his eyes behold, his eyelids test the sons of men.”
His eyes run to and fro through the whole earth to show himself strong for those whose heart is whole toward him.
The seven, “they are the eyes of Yahweh, which run to and fro through the whole earth”.
“The eyes of Yahweh are toward the righteous”; quoted in 1Pe 3:12.
That your eyes may be open toward this house night and day.
He kept Jacob “as the pupil (אִישׁוֹן) of his eye”.
“He who touches you touches the pupil (בָּבַת) of his eye.”

senses.gloss: look, gleam, appearance; the visible face of the land
senses.definition: The eye of a thing is how it looks: its colour or gleam, how a plague looks on skin or cloth, and the visible surface of the land.

evidence.note: “Its eye (וְעֵינוֹ) was as the eye of bdellium”: the manna's look.
Wine when it is red, “when it gives its eye in the cup”: its sparkle.
The locusts “shall cover the eye of the land, so that one cannot see the land”.
The plague “stood in its eye”: kept its appearance.
The plague has not changed its eye.
A people that “covers the eye of the land”.
“As the eye of חַשְׁמַל out of the midst of the fire.”

senses.definition: A spring rising from the ground, where water is found in the wilderness and drawn by a town; and the springs of the deep.

evidence.note: The angel of Yahweh found Hagar “by the spring of water (עֵין הַמַּיִם) in the wilderness, by the spring on the way to Shur”.
“I stand by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city come out to draw water.”
She went down to the spring, filled her jar and came up.
At Elim were twelve springs of water (עֵינֹת מַיִם) and seventy palms.
A land of brooks of water, of springs and deeps.
When he made strong the springs of the deep.
“The spring of Jacob”: Jacob's descendants as water rising in a land of grain and wine.
Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel.
The Spring Gate of Jerusalem.
Hezekiah stopped the waters of the springs outside the city.

evidence.locator: Exo.21.24, עַיִן → ὀφθαλμόν; Isa.6.10 → ὀφθαλμούς, ὀφθαλμοῖς; Psa.118.23 → ὀφθαλμοῖς; ὀφθαλμός renders עַיִן ×491

evidence.note: “Eye for eye and tooth for tooth”, quoting Exo 21:24; Lev 24:20; Deu 19:21.
Isa 6:10: “their eyes they have closed, lest they see with their eyes”.
Deu 29:3 with Isa 29:10: “eyes that they should not see”.
Psa 118:23: “it is marvellous in our eyes”.
“Eye has not seen”, from Isa 64:3.
Psa 34:16: “the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous”.
The Lamb's seven eyes, “the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth”, from Zec 4:10.

evidence.locator: Pro.3.4, בְּעֵינֵי → ἐνώπιον; ἐνώπιον renders עַיִן ×56 (ἐναντίον ×62, as Gen.6.8)

evidence.note: “Provide things honest in the sight of all men”, from Pro 3:4.
“Not only in the sight of the Lord but also in the sight of men”: Pro 3:4.

evidence.locator: Gen.16.7, עֵין, עַיִן → πηγῆς; πηγή renders עַיִן ×13

evidence.note: “Jacob's spring (πηγὴ τοῦ Ἰακώβ)” at Sychar; compare עֵין יַעֲקֹב, Deu 33:28.
“The spring of the water of life.”

parallels.note: “Ear”: eye and ear together for perception and understanding.
“Heart”: the eyes go astray after the heart, and the heart is given with the eyes.
“Deep”: the springs beside the deeps from which they rise.

opposites.note: Man sees “to the eyes”, the outward look; Yahweh sees to the heart.
The blind, whose eyes are opened or for whom another is eyes.

words.summary: A noun formed with מ from עַיִן “spring”: a spring or fountain of water, mostly in poetry and prophecy. The fountains of the great deep, broken open at the flood, are its first use; it is also the figure of a source of life and blessing. Plural מַעְיָנוֹת and מַעְיָנִים.

senses.definition: Water rising from the ground and running: a spring, which stays clean where a cistern or pool would not, which can be stopped up in war, and which God sends into the valleys or brings out of rock.

evidence.note: “A מַעְיָן or a cistern, a gathering of water, shall be clean.”
“He sends springs into the valleys; they go between the hills.”
They stopped every spring of water.
“To all the springs of water and to all the wadis.”
“You split open spring and wadi.”
Flint turned into a spring of water.
The spring of the waters of Nephtoah, a border mark.

senses.gloss: the fountains of the great deep
senses.definition: The springs of the waters under the earth, which were there before the hills (Pro 8:24) and which broke open at the flood together with the windows of heaven, and were closed again.

evidence.note: “All the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the windows of heaven were opened.”
“The fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven were closed.”
“When there were no springs heavy with water”, before creation.

senses.gloss: fountain as a figure: source of life and blessing
senses.definition: A spring as the figure of what gives life: salvation drawn with joy, the spring that goes out from Yahweh's house, the bride as a sealed fountain, a man's own wife; a righteous man who gives way before the wicked is a fouled spring.

evidence.note: “With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.”
“A spring will go out from the house of Yahweh and water the valley of Shittim.”
Of Zion: “all my springs are in you”.
Passing through the valley of Baca they make it a spring.
“Should your springs be scattered abroad?”: a man's waters are for his own wife (5:15, 18).
“A spring shut up, a fountain sealed.”
“A trampled spring and a ruined fountain is a righteous man giving way before the wicked.”
Ephraim's spring dries up under the east wind of Yahweh.

evidence.locator: Gen.7.11, מַעְיְנֹת → πηγαί; Isa.12.3, מַעַיְנֵי → πηγῶν; πηγή renders מַעְיָן ×18

evidence.note: The water Jesus gives becomes “a spring of water welling up to everlasting life”: the wells of salvation of Isa 12:3.
The Lamb leads them to living springs of waters.
False teachers “springs without water”.

parallels.note: “Wadi, torrent”: springs and wadis together as a land's water.
“Fountain, source”, beside it in parallel lines.
“A spring shut up”, beside “a fountain sealed”.

phrases.gloss: the fountains of the great deep

words.summary: A verb made from the noun, found once: the qal participle עוֹיֵן (written עון), of Saul watching David with a jealous eye after the women's song. One use, fixed by its context.

senses.definition: To keep an eye on someone as a rival: Saul, angry that the women ascribed tens of thousands to David, “was eyeing David from that day on”.

evidence.note: וַיְהִי שָׁאוּל עוֹיֵן אֶת־דָּוִד מֵהַיּוֹם הַהוּא וָהָלְאָה.
The cause: the saying “was evil in his eyes”; “what more can he have but the kingdom?”
Saul became David's enemy continually.

greek.gloss: look askance at, eye with suspicion

words.summary: Scripture's Aramaic word for the eye, in Daniel and Ezra; the same uses as the Hebrew: the eyes lifted to heaven, and the eye of God watching over his people.

senses.definition: The eye: lifted to heaven by Nebuchadnezzar as his understanding returned, set in the little horn “like the eyes of a man”, and the eye of God on the elders of the Jews.

evidence.note: “I lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding returned to me.”
“Eyes like the eyes of a man in this horn.”
“The eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews”, so the work was not stopped: the same watchful care as Hebrew עֵינֵי יַהְוֶה.

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܥܝܢܐ (ʿaynā), for ὀφθαλμός throughout the New Testament; in Revelation (a later Syriac translation printed with the Peshitta) it is also the spring of water, as Hebrew עַיִן is both.

senses.definition: The eye, with the Hebrew idioms carried over: the eye that causes stumbling, the eye as the lamp of the body, the evil (grudging) eye, “marvellous in our eyes”, the eyes of the Lord.

evidence.note: “Eye for eye”, quoting Exo 21:24.
“The lamp of the body is the eye; if your eye is single, your whole body is full of light.”
“If your eye is evil.”
“Is your eye evil because I am good?”
An evil eye among the things that come out of the heart.
“It is marvellous in our eyes”, Psa 118:23.
“The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous”, Psa 34:16.
All things naked and laid open to his eyes.

senses.definition: A spring or fountain of water, in Revelation's Syriac.

evidence.note: He will lead them to springs of living water, and wipe every tear from their eyes: the word twice in one verse, once for each sense.
The star fell on the rivers and springs of waters.

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܡܥܝܢܐ (maʿyānā), formed as Hebrew מַעְיָן: a spring, and the source of a flow.

senses.definition: A spring of water, Jacob's at Sychar and the one Jesus gives within; and the source of a flow, the fountain of the woman's blood that dried up.

evidence.note: Jacob's spring, where Jesus sat.
“A spring of water welling up to everlasting life.”
“The fountain of her blood was dried up.”
“Springs without water.”

cognates.gloss: eye; look, view; spring of water; (form III ʿāyana) see with one's own eye
cognates.note: Lane's sources give the eye, the organ of sight, as the primary sense, and from it the spring “of water that wells forth from the earth and runs”, “likened to the organ [of sight] because of the water that is in it”; also a look or view, the evil eye, and “sight with the eye”. Form III ʿāyantuhu “I saw it with my eye”, ʿiyān “ocular view”. The verb ʿāna “smite with the [evil] eye” answers to עוֹיֵן (1Sa 18:9). muʿtān is “an explorer of a people … sent before to seek for herbage and water and the places where rain has fallen”, which is what Hobab was asked to be to Israel (Num 10:31). Arabic ع (ʿ), not غ (ġ), stands behind ע.

evidence.note: “العَيْنُ signifies The eye: the organ of sight” … “The عَيْن, or source, or spring, of water, that wells forth from the earth, or ground, and runs”; “Look, or view”.
“The smiting with the [evil] eye”; form III “I saw it [or him] with my eye”.
“An explorer of a people or party, who is sent before to seek for herbage and water and the places where rain has fallen.”

cognates.note: Very common (over 2,800 attestations in Oracc's glossaries), for both the eye and the spring or source of water, as Hebrew עַיִן. Akkadian lost ʿ, so it cannot show which older sound stood behind ע.

evidence.note: “(water)source; eye; eye(-stone); opening; spring; well.”

cognates.note: Ugaritic keeps ʿ and ġ apart and writes this word with ʿ. Dual ʿnm “eyes”; ʿn also “spring, well”, of women drawing water.

evidence.note: du. ʿnm (KTU 1.2:IV:22), ʿnk (1.16:I:27) “eye”; ʿn (1.12:II:59; 1.100:1) “spring, well”.

cognates.gloss: spring; (dual) eyes; lʿn “in the eyes of”, on the part of; ʿn ʾš “in public view”
cognates.note: Phoenician has the spring (the Spring of YDLL, KAI 14), the eyes, and the same idioms as Hebrew: lʿn ʾlnm wbn ʾdm, favour “in the eyes of gods and men” (KAI 48; KAI 10), as Hebrew מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי אֱלֹהִים וְאָדָם (Pro 3:4); and a stele set up “in public view”, as לְעֵינֵי.

evidence.locator: p. 380, ʿN I and ʿN ʾŠ
evidence.note: ʿN I “n.f. SPRING”, KAI 14.16/17; ʿN ʾŠ “IN PUBLIC VIEW”, KAI 60.4/5.
“n.f. dual 1. EYES … 2. IN (PUBLIC) VIEW”, KAI 34.
“ON THE PART OF, lit., IN THE EYES OF”: KAI 48.4 “grant them favor and long life on the part of gods and men”; KAI 10.9.

cognates.note: Sabaic, which keeps ʿ and ġ apart: the noun is both the eye (a dedicant thanks the god for healing “the disease her eye suffered”) and “spring of water” (fighting “in the lowlands of the springs”). The verb h-ʿyn, “turn oneself toward”, is from the same root.

evidence.note: n. ʿyn: “(1) EYE … J706/7 … (2) SPRING OF WATER, J665/28”; vb. hʿyn “TURN ONE'S SELF TOWARDS”, C464/4.

cognates.note: Geʿez writes it with ʿ. Beside eye and spring it means a spy, as Tigre does: one who sees for others, as Hobab was to be eyes for Israel (Num 10:31).

evidence.note: Geʿez ʿayn “eye; fountain, spring; … spy”, Tigre the same “spy” (read from the OCR text; page image not checked).

cognates.gloss: eye, sight; evil eye; spring, well (Jewish Aramaic)
cognates.note: The Targums use it for the Hebrew eye (Targ. Lev 24:20) and for the spring (Targ. Gen 16:7), and the later language for the evil eye, as Hebrew רַע עַיִן.

evidence.note: “eye, sight &c. Targ. Lev. XXIV, 20 … ע׳ בישא (or only ע׳) evil eye … spring, well. Targ. Gen. XVI, 7.”

cognates.note: Syriac root ʿyn: ʿaynā “eye” and maʿyānā “source, well, fountain”, the same pair as Hebrew עַיִן and מַעְיָן. The Peshitta New Testament's use of them is given as words of the entry.

evidence.locator: lexemes 2308 E;NA (eye), 2307 ME;NA (source; well; fountain), root 1374 E;N

doctrine.statement: Yahweh's “throne is in heaven”, and from there “his eyes behold, his eyelids test the sons of men” (Psa 11:4); yet “the eyes of Yahweh are in every place, watching the evil and the good” (Pro 15:3) and “run to and fro through the whole earth, to show himself strong for those whose heart is whole toward him” (2Ch 16:9). Zechariah's seven lamps “are the eyes of Yahweh, which run to and fro through the whole earth” (Zec 4:10), and Revelation gives the Lamb “seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth” (Rev 5:6). David asks, “where shall I go from your spirit?” (Psa 139:7). From the verses: God is in heaven, and sees everywhere by his spirit sent out through the earth; nothing is hidden from his sight (Heb 4:13), and his eyes are toward the righteous for their good (Psa 34:16; 1Pe 3:12; Deu 11:12; Ezr 5:5).

“Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” is given in the law as the measure for a court: the penalty is paid “as the judges determine” (Exo 21:22–24); the judges inquire, and if a witness is false they do to him what he meant to do to his brother, “your eye shall not pity: life for life, eye for eye” (Deu 19:18–21); “as he has done, so shall it be done to him” (Lev 24:19–20). The same law forbids a man to avenge himself or bear a grudge against his neighbour, but to love him as himself (Lev 19:18). Jesus cites the words and tells his disciples not to resist the evil man but to turn the other cheek (Mat 5:38–39), and Paul, quoting Deu 32:35, tells them never to avenge themselves but to leave it to wrath, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord” (Rom 12:17–19). From the verses: eye for eye was justice's measure in the judges' hands, never licence for private revenge; the disciple leaves repayment to God.

Moses told Israel, after forty years of signs before their eyes, “Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day” (Deu 29:2–3). Isaiah was sent to a people who would not turn: “shut their eyes, lest they see with their eyes … and turn and be healed” (Isa 6:9–10). Jesus applied this to those who heard his parables and did not understand, and blessed his disciples' eyes “for they see” (Mat 13:13–16); John applied it to those who saw his signs and did not believe (Jhn 12:37–40); Paul to the Jews of Rome (Act 28:25–27) and to Israel that had not obtained what it sought (Rom 11:7–8). The psalmist prays, “uncover my eyes, that I may behold wonderful things out of your law” (Psa 119:18). From the verses: seeing the works and hearing the words is not enough; eyes that see are understanding of God's word, which he gives to those who seek it and withholds from those who harden themselves against it.

The flood's waters came from below as well as above: “on that day all the fountains (מַעְיְנֹת) of the great deep burst open, and the windows of heaven were opened”, and rain fell forty days (Gen 7:11–12); after a hundred and fifty days “the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven were closed, and the rain from heaven was restrained” (Gen 8:2–3). The waters prevailed over “all the high mountains under the whole heaven” (Gen 7:19–20). From the verses: the flood was not a local overflow of rain but the opening of the springs of the deep God had set at creation (Pro 8:24, 28) together with the waters above, covering the whole earth.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Numbers 10 (לְעֵינָיִם, Num 10:31; the name עֵינָן, Num 10:27) and Leviticus 23. The database keys the root עינ as the brief does. BDB keys claimed: p.ck.aa (the noun, eye and spring together), p.ck.at (מַעְיָן), p.ck.ab (the verb), xp.ad.aj (Aramaic). p.ck.ac (BDB's “spring”) holds the same tokens as p.ck.aa plus four En-rogel רֹגֵל and four הַקּוֹרֵא tokens filed by spelling (Jos 15:7; 18:16; 2Sa 17:17; 1Ki 1:9; Jdg 15:19; Isa 6:4; 45:3; Amo 5:8), so only p.ck.aa is named and “spring” is a sense of the one word. The verb's single token (1Sa 18:9, Q עוֹיֵן, K עון) carries no BDB key in the database, so its use count reads 0. xp.ad.aj also gathers seven Hebrew וְעֵין tokens by spelling (Jos 15:34, 62; 19:21 ×2; 19:37; Zec 11:17; Job 24:15); its Aramaic tokens are Dan 4:31; 7:8 ×2; 7:20; Ezr 5:5. Psa 25:15; 123:2), borne by several men (TIPNR Elioenai@1Ch.3.23 etc.), which could take a name entry linked here. Peshitta words found from SEDRA root 1374 via the BFBS word list: ܥܝܢܐ in Revelation means “spring” (Rev 7:17; 8:10; 14:7; 16:4; 21:6); Revelation and 2 Peter in the BFBS text are later Syriac translations, not the original Peshitta canon. Cognates: Segert's page (195 or 196) from the OCR's order, not the page image; Fisher read from OCR only (Geʿez ʿayn “spy” garbled); Krahmalkov from the text layer; Biella from OCR. Leads not followed: Segert's grammar quotes KTU 1.19:III:28–29 “in lifting up his eyes he perceives”, the same idiom as נָשָׂא עֵינָיו וַיַּרְא (page not found in the OCR); Dillmann and Leslau for Geʿez; CAD for Akkadian īnu. Open questions: (1) whether “spring” should be a separate word (BDB files it apart) rather than a sense; (2) whether Lev 13:5, 55 is the plague's “appearance” or its colour; (3) the eyes-of-yahweh doctrine's wording on the spirit.
